title: Guilmet v. Campbell
lead: A patient credited with hearing specific promises about surgery recovered contract damages even though the jury found for the surgeons on malpractice; the justices differed about what the general contract verdict established.

actors.name: Richard Guilmet
actors.role: Patient alleging specific promises about an operation’s result

actors.name: Drs. Campbell and Arena
actors.role: Surgeons defending contract and malpractice counts

actors.name: Dr. Klewicki
actors.role: Treating physician who referred Richard to the surgeons

actors.name: Justices T. G. Kavanagh, T. E. Brennan, and Black
actors.role: Majority author, concurring author, and dissenter

proceedings: Jury found for surgeons on malpractice and awarded plaintiffs $50,000 on contract; trial court denied judgment notwithstanding verdict; Court of Appeals affirmed; Michigan Supreme Court affirmed six to one, with differing rationales.
limits: The 1971 common-law decision did not equate unsuccessful treatment with a guarantee or make a new malpractice finding. The later signed-writing statute discussed by the casebook is distinct legislative history. The report contains differing surgery-date descriptions and no published appendix referenced by Black.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A nonemergency consultation produced disputed assurances about the result
sections.cue: Introduce the patient’s condition and the alleged promise.
paragraphs: Richard Guilmet nearly died from peptic-ulcer bleeding in fall 1963. His treating physician, Dr. Klewicki, referred him to surgeons Drs. Campbell and Arena. At a January 1964 consultation he asked whether to undergo an operation. The majority reported that nobody said he had to, and Campbell testified that Guilmet was in excellent physical condition and the surgery was not an emergency.

Guilmet testified that Campbell said surgery would remove his troubles, allow unrestricted eating and drinking, and restore normal activities. Campbell allegedly called himself and Arena experienced specialists, described a simple operation without danger, predicted four or five hospital days and at most three or four weeks off work, said medication could be discarded, and suggested comparing surgical cost with decades of drugs and visits. Guilmet underwent surgery. The trial judge doubted every attributed statement was made but recognized the jury could credit Guilmet. There was no undisputed written guarantee.

sections.title: Serious complications differed from the asserted undertaking
sections.cue: Preserve the disputed causal account and separate verdicts.
paragraphs: The majority described a ruptured-esophagus diagnosis associated with surgical trauma during vagotomy, additional drainage-tube procedures, hepatitis Campbell thought probably related to transfusions, severe coughing and vomiting, and weight loss from 170 to 88 pounds. Guilmet could no longer maintain his former work and recreation. Testimony indicated one infection could recur for up to twenty years. Justice Black’s dissent disputed the esophageal causal account and emphasized evidence of possible spontaneous postoperative perforation.

Richard and Dorothy Guilmet sued in contract and negligence. The contract count alleged an undertaking to cure the stomach problem, unskillful performance, inadequate postoperative care, and failure of satisfactory results. The trial court denied a directed verdict. The jury found for the surgeons on malpractice and awarded the plaintiffs $50,000 on contract. The court denied judgment notwithstanding that verdict; the Court of Appeals affirmed. The Supreme Court reviewed whether the contract verdict had sufficient support, not whether to find negligence anew. The dissent’s $365,000 figure was the demand, not the award.

sections.title: The majority treated the alleged promises as terms of the operation agreement
sections.cue: Explain consideration, specificity, and the factfinder’s role.
paragraphs: Justice T. G. Kavanagh rejected a requirement of a separate special contract with separate consideration. The plaintiffs said the assurances were offered before accepting the operation agreement and formed terms of that same bargain. Unlike a later independent promise, those alleged preacceptance warranties raised no past-consideration problem.

The jury could determine disputed words, intended commitments, acceptance and reliance, the promised result, and failure to deliver it. The surgeons maintained that they promised ordinary professional care and judgment rather than a guarantee. That disagreement depended on context and credibility. The majority declined to make the label “cure” decisive when the parties had not used it; replacing one condition with another need not deliver the described result.

Therapeutic encouragement did not automatically become a contract merely because treatment disappointed. A medical relationship differed from ordinary retail dealing, and the factfinder had to consider that context. Recovery required a specific, clear, express promise to cure or achieve an identified result, reasonably contemplated by both sides and relied on by the patient. The evidence permitted that finding here, making judgment notwithstanding the verdict inappropriate.

sections.title: Brennan agreed on affirmance without identifying a necessary cure guarantee
sections.cue: Keep the general-verdict rationale separate from the majority’s.
paragraphs: Justice T. E. Brennan concurred in affirmance but disputed that the verdict necessarily meant a guaranteed cure despite nonnegligent conduct. The contract count also alleged promised care and skill, and the jury returned a general verdict. In his view, the trial judge’s oral clarification that there was “no negligence” did not turn it into a special verdict or confine the contractual basis.

The judge had removed several allegations from the tort count for insufficient evidence of departure from community standards but had not similarly narrowed the contract count. Brennan therefore thought promised care and skill could support the result without encouraging transformation of routine reassurance into a guarantee. Justices Adams and Williams joined this concurrence as well as the majority, whose reasoning remained distinct.

sections.title: Black would let the defense malpractice verdict defeat the pleaded contract theory
sections.cue: Include the evidentiary objections and final addendum.
paragraphs: Justice Black would reverse and direct judgment for the surgeons. He read the contract claim as charging negligent performance of the same acts as the tort claim, defeated by the jury’s finding of no negligence. He disputed that spontaneous-perforation testimony established negligent esophageal injury and explained that an allegedly forgotten clamp was an intentionally retained surgical clip. He distinguished precedents with different pleadings or separately supported arrangements and warned that medical encouragement could create contract exposure beyond malpractice limitation periods.

His published June 21, 1971 addendum responded to revisions. He expressly recognized deletion of an earlier majority statement that failure of a promised result constituted breach regardless of skill. That withdrawn language was not part of the final majority. The addendum continued to contest the contractual theory and broad assignment of oral-agreement questions to juries, concluding with a vote to reverse and remand for defense judgment. An earlier proposed opinion he referenced as an available-on-request appendix was not included in the published report.

sections.title: The $50,000 judgment stood under the historical rule
sections.cue: State the votes and separate later legislation from adjudication.
paragraphs: Five Justices joined T. G. Kavanagh’s opinion; Brennan supplied an additional vote to affirm, while Black dissented. Adams and Williams also joined Brennan’s concurrence. The six-to-one judgment affirmed the $50,000 recovery and allowed plaintiffs to tax costs. It ordered no new trial, increased no damages, and made no new malpractice finding.

The casebook later reports Michigan’s adoption, three years afterward, of a signed-writing requirement for medical cure promises. That legislative response was not part of the 1971 holding or a certification of the present statute’s scope.
